name: Birhor
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive descriptions checked: Jora & Anderson 2017 is on spatial deixis/serialization (Indian Linguistics 77), Roy 1925 is ethnography, Grierson 1906 a short LSI notice; no phonology with stress located.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid page birh1242; RWAAI (Lund) Birhor collection node lat:10050_00_0000_0000_0003_A6AE_4; OLAC/ELAR/Shodhganga/CiNii/OpenAlex/Crossref/archive.org/HathiTrust searches.
sources.note: No grammar, phonology or sketch of Birhor located anywhere: Glottolog lists only Jora & Anderson 2017 as descriptive; RWAAI has an empty Birhor node; ELAR has no Birhor deposit; Shodhganga returns only anthropology theses (none linguistic); Bikram Jora's Delhi University PhD (2014, per Living Tongues bio) has no locatable title or copy.

sources.citation: Anderson, Gregory D. S. & Bikram Jora. 2021. Introduction to the templatic verb morphology of Birhor (Birhoɽ), a Kherwarian Munda language. Language and Linguistics 22(1): 1-27. doi:10.1075/lali.00076.and (CC BY 4.0).
sources.note: Nothing. a full-text search for stress/accent/syllab returns only 'prosodic and morphotactic characteristics' of agreement markers (p. 3), the count of 'phonological words' in verb templates (pp. 9-10), and a historical 'minimal word constraint' remark (p. 17). No phoneme inventory, no stress statement.

sources.citation: Anderson, Gregory D. S. & Bikram Jora. 2017. The linguistic ecology of 'particularly vulnerable tribal' groups in Middle India: State-mediated ethnolinguistic erasure and neocolonialist 'development' (SALSA paper; Birhoɽ and Gtaʔ).
sources.note: Nothing; sociolinguistic paper. Says 'Very little data has appeared on Birhor to date' beyond the LSI specimen and a small lexical set.

sources.citation: Roy, Sarat Chandra. 1925. The Birhors: a little-known jungle tribe of Chota Nagpur. Ranchi: G. E. L. Mission Press. Ch. II 'Language' pp. 59-61; Appendix I 'Birhor Vocabulary' pp. 559-591.
sources.note: Nothing. Ethnography with a short language note (Birhor closer to Mundari than Santali, some Santali-like features) and a wordlist; the author writes 'I shall not enter into details of the grammatical structure' (p. 561). No accent or stress statement.

sources.citation: Grierson, George A. (ed.). 1906. Linguistic Survey of India, vol. IV: Munda and Dravidian languages. Calcutta: Office of the Superintendent of Government Printing. 'Birhar' notice and Prodigal Son specimen, pp. 102-105.
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library, call number 3254.1 F; Linguistics Library, call number CoPh 5.40; a Harvard library, call number Ud 0010
sources.note: The Birhar section has one 'Pronunciation' paragraph (vowel distinctions, cerebral r) and no accent statement; it says 'In Ranchi it does not differ much from Mundari'. Accent statements in the volume are for Santali ('In words of two syllables the accent usually rests on the first..') and Mundari ('Accent.—The accent is the same as in Santali'), not for Birhar.

sources.citation: Pradhan, Sabita, Arimardan Kumar Tripathi & Akash Bhagat. 2022. Birhor: Language and Life. Santiniketan: Centre for Endangered Languages, Visva-Bharati. 146 pp. ISBN 978-81-957226-6-2. (Grammatical sketch ch. 7, pp. 50-59: 7.1 Phonology pp. 50-53; based on fieldwork in four Birhor villages of Purulia district, West Bengal.)

tone.summary: Nothing stated: segmental inventory only; tone and stress not mentioned.

sources.citation: Anderson, Gregory D. S., Bikram Jora, Sashi Kant Lakra, Anukaran Marki & Biswanath Birhor. 2022. A Trilingual Dictionary of Birhoɽ: Birhoɽ-Hindi-English. Salem, OR: Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages.

sources.note: The only modern first-hand lexical description with IPA; its front matter is the most likely place for a phoneme inventory and a stress/orthography note. Living Tongues says its PDFs are available on request.
sources.venue: Salem, OR: Living Tongues Institute for Endangered Languages

tone.summary: Trilingual dictionary; its Introduction (pp. II-III) treats only vowels, nasalization, length, nasals and the glottal stop. No word on tone, pitch or stress in the pages available (14 of 80).

sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog mund1335). No text seen: a comparative/reconstructive chapter on Proto-Munda prosody (word-level weak-strong pattern), morphotactics and morphosyntax by the fieldworker who holds the Birhor data; it may cite Kherwarian (possibly Birhor) forms for the prosodic word, but no abstract or text is exposed anywhere reachable, so no tone or stress statement about Birhor can be attributed to it.

sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog mund1335). No text seen: a 50-page family-level overview of the Munda languages (Birhor is one of the Kherwarian lects it classifies); expected to carry Anderson's comparative remarks on Munda word prosody (Kherwarian second-syllable/iambic prominence, lexical tone only in Korku among North Munda), but whether Birhor is named in any prosody passage is unverified; no abstract is exposed (Semantic Scholar: abstract elided by publisher; Brill landing bot-walled).
